item.title: 14 Boeing aircraft: Buying more than planes
item.description:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines is set to acquire 14 new Boeing aircraft. At around $3.7 billion, the decision has naturally attracted debate. Some question whether Bangladesh, given its present economic pressures, should make an investment of this size. Others see it largely through a political lens, with criticism extending to the government itself.

But to look at the purchase only in terms of its immediate cost would miss the larger question: where does Bangladesh want to see its national airline 20 years from now?

We often speak of Emirates and Qatar Airways. Dubai and Doha did not become global aviation hubs simply by building modern airports. Their success came through years of investment in aircraft, routes and connectivity, eventually creating a business that carries passengers not only to their home countries but through them to the rest of the world.

Bangladesh is different, and the comparison should not be taken too far. But there is a lesson here. Aviation is a long-term business. Investments made today may be intended for markets that will take a decade or more to develop.

Seen from that perspective, Biman’s plan deserves a more considered assessment. The proposed fleet includes eight Boeing 787-10s, two 787-9s and four 737-8s, intended for a combination of Middle Eastern, regional and long-haul routes. Deliveries are expected to begin towards the end of 2031 and continue until 2035.

The timeline matters. Bangladesh is making a decision today about the aviation market it expects to compete in during the 2030s and beyond.
There is also an economic argument for acting early. No one can say with certainty what comparable aircraft will cost five years from now. Inflation, production costs, technology, supply chains and long delivery cycles all influence aircraft prices.

If similar aircraft were to cost even 20 or 30 percent more in five years, securing commercial terms and production slots earlier could itself provide a significant procurement advantage. This does not mean such an increase is certain. It simply means that the cost of waiting should also be part of the calculation.

Biman’s financial position is relevant too. In FY2024-25, the airline reported Tk 11,559 crore in revenue, Tk 1,602 crore in operating profit and more than Tk 785 crore in net profit. It carried around 3.4 million passengers and earned Tk 925 crore from cargo. A company that has remained profitable for five consecutive years must eventually decide whether to maintain its present position or invest in expansion.

Operationally, there is another advantage. Biman already flies Boeing 787s and 737s. Existing experience in pilot training, engineering, maintenance and spare-parts management can therefore support the expanded fleet. Improved fuel efficiency could also produce substantial savings over an aircraft’s operating life.

The purchase also sits within the wider Bangladesh-US commercial relationship. The proposed Boeing acquisition is connected to a broader trade framework involving market access and other economic commitments. To view it only through Biman’s balance sheet would therefore leave out part of the picture.

None of this means the deal should escape scrutiny. A multibillion-dollar investment demands transparency. The final negotiated price, financing cost, repayment period, route strategy and expected aircraft utilisation should all be clear. If sovereign guarantees are involved, accountability becomes even more important.

Fleet expansion is fine, but its success will depend on what happens after the aircraft arrive. Buying planes alone will not turn Biman into Emirates or Qatar Airways. The harder task will be keeping them in the air, filling their seats, carrying profitable cargo, opening the right routes and gradually making Dhaka a competitive connecting point.

Bangladesh cannot aspire to build a serious international airline while planning only a few years ahead.

Ultimately, the debate should not end with the $3.7 billion price tag. The real question is whether Bangladesh can turn these 14 aircraft into a profitable aviation business for the next 20 years.

item.title: Fertiliser dealer’s warehouse vandalised in Kurigram, roadblock in Lalmonirhat
item.description:
Angry farmers vandalised a fertiliser dealer’s warehouse at Kachakata Bazar in Nageshwari upazila of Kurigram, after the distribution of fertiliser was delayed.

Farmers also staged a road blockade in Bhurungamari upazila of the district demanding fertiliser. In Lalmonirhat, farmers likewise blocked a road and staged demonstrations over the same demand.

Local farmers said they began gathering outside Kashem Traders, a fertiliser dealer at Kachakata Bazar in Nageshwari, from 7:00 am to collect fertiliser. As the dealer’s representatives had still not arrived after 8:00 am, frustration grew among the farmers waiting there. At one point, around 200 farmers had gathered. At about 9:00 am, the farmers began shouting and protesting. Several of them then vandalised part of the warehouse’s corrugated-tin fencing. However, local farmers said no fertiliser was taken from the warehouse as others intervened.

Several farmers said tensions escalated because the dealer’s representatives failed to arrive for a long time despite fertiliser being available at the warehouse. Pushing and jostling broke out among the farmers, after which some of them damaged the corrugated-tin fencing.

Arpan Kumar Das, officer-in-charge of Kachakata police station, told Prothom Alo that the dealer had sufficient fertiliser in the warehouse.

He said the farmers became angry because the dealer arrived somewhat late. During pushing and jostling among 150 to 200 people, sections of the warehouse’s corrugated-tin fencing were damaged.

Police later arrived, brought the situation under control and distributed the fertiliser. The situation is now normal, he added.

Meanwhile, farmers blocked a road at Milan Bazar in Baladia Union of Bhurungamari after failing to obtain fertiliser. Traffic on the road was halted for some time. Police went to the scene after being informed.

Later, Upazila Assistant Commissioner (Land) Aminul Haque Tareque arrived at the scene and spoke with the farmers, after which the situation returned to normal.

Aminul Haque Tareque told Prothom Alo that farmers from surrounding areas had gathered after hearing that fertiliser would be distributed from a warehouse at Milan Bazar. This brought traffic on the road to a standstill. The warehouse had 20 tonnes of fertiliser, but distribution was not possible that day because of the large number of farmers.

An additional supply of fertiliser would be brought in the following day and distributed together, he said.

Road blockade in Lalmonirhat

Angry farmers blocked a highway in Lalmonirhat by placing tree trunks on the road, demanding an adequate supply of fertiliser and an end to the alleged “fertiliser syndicate”.

The blockade was staged at around 11:00 am today in the Mahendranagar Bazar area of Lalmonirhat Sadar on the Lalmonirhat–Patgram–Burimari highway. Traffic on the highway remained halted for around an hour.

The protesting farmers later withdrew the blockade following intervention by the district administration and assurances that fertiliser supplies would be ensured.

The protesting farmers alleged that they had been unable to apply fertiliser to their fields on time during the ongoing Aman cultivation season because they had not received adequate supplies according to demand.

They also said they were forced to take to the national highway to demand a regular supply of fertiliser and an end to the artificial shortage or alleged syndicate surrounding its distribution.

Upon receiving the news, Lalmonirhat Deputy Commissioner Md Rashedul Haque Pradhan, Superintendent of Police Md Asaduzzaman, Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mononita Das and local Mahendranagar Union Parishad chairman Md Abdul Majid Mondal quickly arrived at the scene.

They assured the farmers that positive steps would be taken to address their demands, following which the protesters left the road.

Addressing the farmers, Deputy Commissioner Md Rashedul Haque Pradhan said there was essentially no shortage of fertiliser in Lalmonirhat district.

He said a misunderstanding had temporarily arisen after a large number of farmers from Lalmonirhat Sadar gathered at Mahendranagar upon hearing that fertiliser was being distributed in a union in Hatibandha.

He added that if any specific allegation of an artificial fertiliser shortage was received, the authorities would investigate it and take immediate and strict administrative action.

item.title: Study: What children watch matters more than screen time
item.description:
What children do on screens, and whether parents engage with them, may matter more for language development than simply how many hours they spend on digital devices, according to a study that also reveals widespread passive screen use and limited parental involvement among young children.
Titled “Effect of using screen time in developing children’s speech and language: Bangladesh context,” the MPhil study was conducted by Md Zahid Hossain Khan of Dhaka University’s Department of Communication Disorders under the supervision of Professor Dr Hakim Arif.
The study found that 60% of children surveyed spent at least three hours a day on screens, while 80% primarily watched cartoons and other entertainment content.
Yet only 20% of parents consistently stayed with their children during screen use, highlighting a major gap in how digital devices are being incorporated into children’s daily lives.
Researchers found a striking contrast between un-interative viewing and interactive screen use.
Children aged three to five who used educational and interactive apps repeated new words, asked questions and demonstrated improvements in sentence formation.
Those who mainly watched cartoons or YouTube videos, however, showed less inclination to communicate, with some crying or becoming stubborn when the screen was taken away.
The findings challenge the tendency to judge children’s digital exposure solely by the number of hours spent in front of screens, suggesting that the quality of content, active participation and parental interaction can be critical factors.
The research covered 50 children aged three to eight and an equal number of parents and caregivers in Dhaka, Chittagong and Tangail.
In addition to a survey, researchers directly observed each child for 30 minutes while they used a screen.
The findings show that 40% of the children spent three to four hours a day on screens, while another 20% spent more than four hours.
Mobile phones dominated their digital exposure, used by 90% of the children.
Television was used by 70% and tablets by 50%.
Around 80% primarily watched cartoons and entertainment programs, while 60% of children spend time sitting inactive in front of screens rather than actively interacting with the content.
Among children aged six to eight, researchers observed greater discussion about what they watched, although their sentence structures were comparatively weak.
The study also identified parental involvement as a key concern.
Only one in five parents always accompanied their children during screen use, while just 30% actively regulated screen time.
Half of the parents surveyed believed excessive screen use negatively affected language development, while 60% reported a decline in their children’s vocabulary.
At the same time, 60% believed screens could help children learn language when used appropriately.
“Two-way conversation is a key condition for language learning, while screens can turn communication into a one-way process,” Zahid said.
“If parents sit beside their children and talk about the content, screen time is no longer merely screen time; it becomes part of the learning process.”
The findings therefore suggest that parental engagement can change the nature of screen exposure: rather than children simply consuming content, conversation, questions and responses can turn it into an interactive learning experience.
Professor Saiful Alam Chowdhury of the University of Chittagong said the study recommended age-appropriate limits on screen use, development and promotion of quality educational content in Bangla, training for parents and teachers, and government-led awareness programs.
Professor Dr Hakim Arif said children’s growing exposure to screens had emerged as a major challenge to healthy development.
“There has been little long-term scientific research on the issue in our society. I believe this research will play an important role in addressing that gap,” he said.
The findings point to a broader challenge for parents as digital devices become increasingly embedded in childhood: managing screen use may no longer be simply about limiting hours, but also about determining what children watch, how they interact with it and whether adults remain engaged in the process.

item.title: Expressway murder: Bus supervisor, assistant confess, driver remanded
item.description:
Two employees of a Raj Classic bus arrested in connection with the murder of a man whose body was found with his mouth taped shut on the Dhaka Elevated Expressway have given confessional statements before a court, while the bus driver has been placed on four days’ remand for questioning.
The arrested bus supervisor, Saju Laskar, and his assistant, Mahbub Alam Monir, voluntarily gave confessional statements before separate magistrates and were subsequently sent to jail.
The court also granted four days’ remand for bus driver Sohel Rana, who was arrested in connection with the killing of Ismail Hossain.
The case’s investigating officer, Banani Police Station Sub-Inspector Nazrul Islam Talukdar, produced the three accused before the court, seeking to record the confessional statements of Saju and Monir and a seven-day remand for Sohel.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Albiruni Mir recorded Saju’s statement, while Metropolitan Magistrate Md Siddiq Azad recorded Monir’s statement. Both were later sent to jail.
Following a hearing, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam granted four days’ remand for Sohel. Sub-Inspector Moktar Hossain of the prosecution division confirmed the matter.
According to the case statement, Ismail left his home in Jamalpur at around 4:30am on September 4 for his residence in Gazipur. He was carrying Tk500,000 in cash from the sale of family land, along with various food items.
His son, Md Hasan, waited for him at Jirani Bus Stand in Gazipur. When repeated calls to his father’s mobile phone went unanswered, Hasan waited until around 10am before returning home.
At around noon, Banani Police Station informed a neighbour that Ismail’s body had been found. Hasan later identified his father from photographs.
Police recovered Ismail’s body from the Dhaka Elevated Expressway between pillars 179 and 180 on the Kakoli-Kuril-bound carriageway in Banani.
The Tk500,000 in cash and other belongings he had been carrying were missing. His body bore injury marks, while his nose, head and right wrist were wrapped with white packing tape.
Hasan filed a murder case with Banani Police Station on September 4.

item.title: Shama: Rohingya verification must not delay repatriation
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Sunday called for expediting verification of Rohingyas under existing bilateral arrangements with Myanmar, saying the process cannot become an open-ended administrative exercise delaying actual repatriation.
"Verification cannot become an open-ended administrative exercise. We need to expedite verification on the basis of the existing bilateral arrangements," she said.
Shama made the remarks while addressing, as a special guest, a roundtable discussion titled "The Rohingya Crisis: Emerging Challenges and Reframing Response Strategies", organised by The Institute for Global Cooperation Foundation (IGCF), at the Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) auditorium in the capital.
The state minister said Bangladesh, in its bilateral engagement with Myanmar, has prioritised accelerating the verification process to move towards actual repatriation.
She stressed the need to address practical realities involving Rohingyas born in the camps as well as those who have arrived from Rakhine State since 2017.
Shama said Bangladesh's diplomatic efforts are aimed at maintaining international attention on the protracted crisis, strengthening humanitarian support, promoting accountability and, above all, creating conducive conditions for the Rohingyas to return home.
She warned that Bangladesh is finding it increasingly difficult to sustain its humanitarian responsibilities amid declining international funding.
"Bangladesh will continue to fulfill its humanitarian responsibilities, but humanitarian support is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain as international funding declines," she said.
Dhaka is therefore urging donors and international partners to scale up their support to protect the lives of the displaced Rohingya population, she continued.
The state minister, however, stressed that humanitarian assistance should be managed carefully so that support provided in the camps does not inadvertently encourage further displacement or complicate prospects for eventual return.
Shama said the key to sustainable repatriation ultimately lies in creating appropriate conditions in Myanmar's Rakhine State.
"We need security there; we need respect for identity and rights there. We need legal recognition for Rohingya there. We need freedom of movement there, and we need access to livelihoods, education, and healthcare," she added.
The state minister for Foreign Affairs said returning Rohingyas must also have confidence that repatriation would not expose them to another cycle of displacement.
Dialogue aimed at reconciliation is necessary to achieve this, she said, seeking stronger engagement from the international community.
Shama called upon the United Nations, ASEAN, development partners and other international stakeholders to support practical confidence-building as well as humanitarian and development initiatives in Rakhine state.
Such engagement, she said, could help prepare the ground for repatriation while addressing the concerns of both returning Rohingyas and host communities in Rakhine.
The state minister said accountability must remain an integral part of efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis.
Bangladesh continues to support international accountability mechanisms, including proceedings before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Gambia v. Myanmar case, she said.
"Justice is not separate from repatriation; accountability and sustainable return must reinforce each other," Shama said.
She outlined a multidimensional diplomatic strategy involving bilateral engagement with Myanmar, stronger engagement through the UN, regional cooperation involving ASEAN and other partners, humanitarian and development initiatives in Rakhine and sustained international attention to accountability and the root causes of the crisis.
"But the objective must remain singular: to enable the Rohingyas to return home with safety and dignity," she said.
Shama said Bangladesh has already demonstrated humanity, patience and diplomatic commitment in dealing with the crisis, while its past experience showed that repatriation is achievable.
She said the challenge now is to combine political will at home, diplomatic engagement abroad and humanitarian assistance during the transition and concrete measures towards repatriation.
The state minister also said another important conference on the Rohingya crisis would be held on the sidelines of the upcoming United Nations General Assembly, where Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would participate.
Expressing optimism about ultimately resolving the crisis, Shama called for a transition "from protracted displacement to dignified return, from crisis management to crisis resolution, and from uncertainty to hope". Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed spoke as the chief guest while Prime Minister's Adviser on Public Administration Md Ismail Zabihullah delivered a speech as the guest of honour.

item.title: 14kg gold seizure: Biman staffer placed on remand
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Sunday placed a Biman Bangladesh Airlines staffer on five-day remand after police seized nearly 14kg of gold allegedly being smuggled through Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Kamal Uddin passed the order against Biman Assistant Technical Helper Md Shoaib Kazi Sajib, 31, after police sought 10 days’ remand in the gold smuggling case.
The case’s investigating officer, Airport police station Inspector (Operations) Sharif Hossain, produced Sajib before the court and sought the remand.
Sajib’s lawyer Md Shahidul Islam sought bail and cancellation of the remand petition.
According to case documents and police, a search was conducted based on a tip-off on September 5 on Biman’s BG-148/AJS flight, which arrived in Dhaka from Dubai via Chittagong.
Members of Customs, National Security Intelligence (NSI), Directorate of Forces Intelligence (DFI) and Criminal Investigation Department (CID), among other agencies, were present during the search.
Police said Sajib was behaving suspiciously inside the aircraft cabin during the search. After noticing junior security officers and other security personnel, he allegedly ran and threw gold bars hidden on his body inside the cabin.
A packet recovered later contained 120 gold bars wrapped in gray cloth.
The bars weighed 13,992 grams, or nearly 14kg, and were 24-carat pure gold, police said. Their estimated market value was Tk25.2 crore.
Sajib is the son of Firoz Kazi of Kachubania village under Amtali police station in Barguna.
Airport police filed the case under Sections 25B(1)(b) and 25D of the Special Powers Act, 1974.
In the remand petition, police claimed Sajib was an active member of an international gold smuggling syndicate and had been illegally bringing gold from abroad while evading customs duties for a long time.
Police said his remand was necessary to identify and arrest the alleged mastermind and other members of the syndicate.

item.title: A deadly toll underestimated: Bangladesh’s fight for clean air amidst a global crisis
item.description:
“For too long, we have been told to choose between economic growth and environmental protection, between today’s priorities and tomorrow’s climate. These are false choices. Air pollution is taking a devastating toll on lives and economies. Last year, air pollution contributed to 6.4 million premature deaths, 5.5 million new cases of childhood asthma, and millions more of diabetes, dementia and heart disease – a toll long underestimated, and borne most heavily by those least able to bear it.”
These words from the United Nations Secretary-General come at a critical time for Bangladesh, which continues to endure a severe crisis of pollution-related mortality.
Infographic on the State of Global Air Report 2025
The statistics are staggering: 61 deaths per 100,000 people in Bangladesh are attributable to fine particulate outdoor air pollution, totaling 63,347 deaths in 2023. This deadly pollutant, known as PM2.5, consists of tiny solid or liquid particles measuring 2.5 micrometers or less in width. With an annual mean exposure of 69.3 µg/m³, the average person in Bangladesh breathes air that exceeds the World Health Organization’s guideline by 14 times.
With every breath, these minute particles—comprising soot, soil dust, sulfates, and other toxins—penetrate deep into the body to damage lungs, hearts, and brains. The deadliest conditions linked to PM2.5 exposure include stroke, heart disease, lung cancer, and lower respiratory infections like pneumonia. High levels of fine particles also contribute to chronic conditions like type 2 diabetes, hinder cognitive development in children, and exacerbate mental health problems.
According to the State of Global Air Report 2025, the crisis is global but highly concentrated. In 2023, India and China each recorded more than 2 million deaths attributable to air pollution, while Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Nigeria each saw over 200,000 total air pollution deaths. Meanwhile, Indonesia, Myanmar, and Egypt each surpassed 100,000 deaths.
As Bangladesh prepares to join the world community to observe on September 7 for the seventh straight year – International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies – the UN Secretary-General made a fervent call: “I urge governments, businesses and investors to choose action now. Let the air we share unite us.”
He says: “The case for action has never been clearer. The science and the economics point in the same direction: every dollar invested in proven clean air solutions returns 15 US dollars in benefits. Reducing air pollution protects health, boosts productivity, and builds more resilient and prosperous societies.”
The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) says, fine particle pollution is a major cause of death from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischemic heart disease, tracheal, bronchus and lung cancer, stroke, lower respiratory infections, type 2 diabetes and neonatal disorders.
Data from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) underscores the specific disease burden in Bangladesh, where outdoor PM2.5 pollution is responsible for a significant percentage of deaths across major health conditions: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (17%), ischemic heart disease (11%), lung cancer (11%), stroke (10%), lower respiratory infections (9%), type 2 diabetes (5%), and neonatal disorders (5%).
While air pollution has been tied to human activity for millennia—evolving from early cooking fires to the coal-choked cities of the Industrial Revolution and modern 20th-century industrialization—its current impacts are profoundly unequal.
Though atmospheric conditions like wind can disperse or trap pollutants across vast distances, the immediate suffering is disproportionately borne by developing nations and their most vulnerable populations: women, children, and the elderly.
As Bangladesh joins the global community this Monday, September 7, to observe the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, the Secretary-General’s call for action carries immense urgency.
"The science and the economics point in the same direction," he noted, emphasizing that every dollar invested in proven clean air solutions returns 15 US dollars in benefits by protecting health, boosting productivity, and building resilient societies.
For Bangladesh to realize these benefits, it must confront the immediate structural drivers of its toxic air: a large fleet of unfit public buses blowing smoke, a systemic lack of law enforcement against illegally run brick kilns, and rampant infrastructure development that routinely ignores pollution protocols.

item.title: Habibur: Four Dhaka bus terminals to be relocated soon to ease traffic jam
item.description:
State Minister for Road Transport and Bridges Habibur Rashid on Sunday said that initiatives have been taken to relocate the four bus terminals at Gabtoli, Mohakhali, Sayedabad and Gulistan soon and to use existing depots as part of efforts easing the city traffic congestions.
He said discussions were also held on expanding an alternative terminal at Gabtoli, removing illegal structures in Narayanganj and Gazipur and improving terminals operated by the city corporations.
The state minister made the remarks while talking to the reporters after a meeting of the national committee to address traffic congestion in Greater Dhaka, held at the Road Transport and Highways Division at the Secretariat.
Habibur Rashid said the meeting initially reviewed how far the policies and action plans adopted to address traffic congestion in the city have been implemented and identified the measures that need to be carried out quickly.
He said emphasis has placed on coordinated action by the relevant agencies to ensure timely implementation of the decisions taken to ease traffic congestion.
The state minister said one of the major causes of traffic congestion in the capital is the excessive pressure of buses and public transport within the city. To reduce this pressure, a plan has been taken to lessen dependence on existing terminals and use of terminals and depots at alternative locations.
“We have terminals for addressing traffic congestion and we are taking initiatives to temporarily use some of the depots we already have. We are looking at using places such as Kanchpur and Purbachal,” he said.
The state minister also said discussions were held on further expanding the Gabtoli bus terminal. Talks were held with the concerned authorities on how the new areas adjacent to Gabtoli could be brought into use quickly. Emphasis is being given on the speedy implementation of such alternative infrastructure to reduce the pressure of public transport at the entry points to the capital.
Habibur Rashid said illegal structures on roads in various areas surrounding the capital including Narayanganj and Gazipur are also among the major causes of traffic congestion. The meeting discussed removing of these structures and making the roads suitable for smooth vehicular movement.
He said it would not be enough to take initiatives only to ease congestion within the capital. Greater importance must also be given to the transport links between Dhaka and the surrounding areas. Necessary measures will therefore be taken to remove obstructions on important roads and highways around Dhaka, evict illegal structures and ensure orderly movement of public transport.
The state minister said detailed discussions at the meeting focused mainly on the four bus terminals. Their existing management, the possibility of relocating them to alternative locations, opportunities to use depots and the role of the concerned city corporations are discussed.
He said initiatives would also be taken to improve terminals managed by the city corporations. Discussions covered establishing bus counters at the terminals, ensuring necessary facilities for passengers and making the transport management more effective.
The meeting also discussed allowing air-conditioned buses, in particular, to use designated terminals. It was decided that the locations and arrangements for bus counters and other necessary facilities would be determined in coordination with the concerned city corporations and transport stakeholders.
The state minister said merely widening roads or constructing new roads would not solve the city’s traffic congestion. Terminal management, bus operations, parking, counter management and the pressure of vehicles entering and leaving the capital must all be considered in an integrated manner.
The meeting reviewed the actual progress of the decisions already taken and placed emphasis on speeding up work in areas where implementation has been slow.
Discussions were also held on increasing coordination among the relevant institutions and completing the work within the stipulated timeframe.
Habibur Rashid said the meeting reviewed the progress of measures adopted under the traffic congestion mitigation policy and assessed how far implementation had advanced. Decisions were taken to move these initiatives forward as quickly as possible and within the appropriate timeframe.
He said the government’s initiatives to ease traffic congestion now need to be implemented with greater momentum. The concerned ministries, city corporations, transport agencies and other stakeholders must work in coordination to achieve this, he added.
A huge number of people in the capital rely on public transport every day. In various areas, the management of bus terminals and counters creates additional pressure on the roads.
In many cases, buses stop on the roads to pick up and drop off passengers, disrupting traffic movement. Officials concerned believe that bringing the terminals under disciplined management could significantly reduce these problems.
According to the government’s plan, necessary infrastructure for public transport will be developed and improved in areas surrounding Dhaka alongside measures to reduce traffic pressure within the city.
This is expected to reduce the improper stopping and parking of buses on major roads and increase traffic flow.
The meeting also discussed future measures in addition to ongoing initiatives to ease congestion in Greater Dhaka. Decisions were taken to undertake necessary administrative and coordination measures to accelerate the implementation of relevant projects and initiatives.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police commissioner, administrators of various city corporations, secretaries and senior officials from the ministry and several other ministries were present at the meeting.

item.title: Mirza Fakhrul visits Thakurgaon for first time as president
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir visited his hometown Thakurgaon on Sunday for the first time since taking office, where he paid respects at his parents’ graves and attended a civic reception.
He was scheduled to arrive by helicopter at the helipad of Thakurgaon Mohammad Ali Stadium at 11:40am but reached the venue around 1pm.
From the stadium, he went to the Thakurgaon District Circuit House, where he received a guard of honor before visiting Senua graveyard to pay respects at his parents’ graves.
The president waved to people gathered along the roads as he traveled through the city.
A civic reception is scheduled for the president at the historic Boro Math of Thakurgaon Government Boys’ High School in the afternoon. People from across the district are expected to attend.
The city has been decorated ahead of the visit, with banners, festoons, arches and lighting installed along major roads, key intersections and entry points.
Residents have expressed pride at seeing someone from Thakurgaon serving as the head of state.
Security has also been tightened across the district, with increased surveillance at important installations, roads and program venues. A large number of law enforcement personnel have been deployed along the president’s route.
On Monday, the president will lay the foundation stone of Thakurgaon University.

item.title: Walton wins ‘ESG Excellence Awards 2026’ in 3 categories
item.description:
Walton has won the ‘ESG Excellence Awards 2026’ in three categories in recognition of its outstanding contributions to ensuring occupational health and safety, taking effective action to combat climate change, and developing innovative and environmentally sustainable products.
The awards, jointly organized by the United Nations Global Compact Network Bangladesh (GCNB) and ESG Institute Bangladesh, recognized Walton in the categories of ‘Excellence in Occupational Health and Safety Improvement,’ ‘Excellence in Championing Climate Action,’ and ‘Excellence in Sustainable Product Innovation.’
Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC received the awards at a gala night titled “ESG Excellence Awards-2026’ held at Lakeshore Hotel in the capital on Saturday (September 5).
Attending as the chief guest, Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo handed over the ‘ESG Awards’ crest to Walton Hi-Tech’s additional managing director (AMD) Mohammad Yousuf Ali.
During that time, Walton Hi-Tech’s chief marketing officer Zoheb Ahmed, senior additional executive directors Rabiul Islam Milton and Md Mostafizur Rahman, and head of EHS and sustainability department Mostafizur Rahman Raju was also present.
Ambassadors of several countries, including Denmark and Sweden, along with representatives from the European Union, GCNB and ESG Institute Bangladesh, also attended the event.
Expressing his reaction to the achievement, Walton Hi-Tech’s AMD Mohammad Yousuf Ali said: “The Walton family is delighted to receive the ‘ESG Excellence Awards-2026’ in three categories. These honours recognize Walton’s effective initiatives and continued progress in ensuring a safe workplace, addressing climate change and sustainable products innovation. The recognition will further inspire us to strengthen future investments and initiatives in environmental protection, employee safety and well-being, and sustainable product innovation alongside business growth.”
“To address climate change, we have significantly reduced carbon emissions through the use of renewable energy at our manufacturing facilities and the adoption of green technologies in production processes,” Yousuf Ali said.
“At the same time, Walton has introduced technology-driven safety management systems and regular training programs to enhance employee awareness. These initiatives are helping prevent workplace accidents while ensuring occupational health and a safer working environment,” he added.
Walton also places particular emphasis on energy efficiency, green technologies and environmentally friendly materials in the development and innovation of sustainable products.
The company said its achievements across these areas have earned special recognition in three categories at the ‘ESG Excellence Awards’.
Earlier this year, Walton also won the ‘SDG Brand Champion Awards 2026’ in three categories, including recognition as the year’s most sustainable electronics manufacturing enterprises, for its contributions to climate and environmental protection as well as clean and energy-efficient technologies.

item.title: Three of a family drown in Lakshmipur
item.description:
Three members of the same family, including two children, drowned in a pond in Lakshmipur’s Sadar upazila on Sunday afternoon.
The deceased were Abu Siddique Patwari, 65, and his grandchildren Piyas, 8, and Prema, 7. The two children were Abu Siddique’s grandson and granddaughter, born to his son and daughter, respectively.
According to locals, Abu Siddique went to the pond at Patwari Bari in Shakchar union to bathe with his grandchildren around noon. At one point, all three drowned and went missing.
Family members later began searching for them and, with the help of locals, recovered their bodies from the pond.
The deaths have cast a pall of grief over the area, with relatives mourning the tragedy.
Wahid Parvez, officer-in-charge of Lakshmipur Sadar Police Station, confirmed the incident, saying police were sent to the scene after receiving the report. Further details would be available later.

item.title: TIB expresses concern over more empowered and unaccountable Battalion
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has expressed concern that the Special Response Battalion (SRB) Bill, 2026, tabled in Parliament with the stated aim of establishing a new specialised police unit following the abolition of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), is in effect being designed to provide a legal basis for a more empowered and virtually unaccountable RAB under a new name.

TIB is deeply concerned that the draft retains provisions granting the SRB broad and ambiguous powers, inadequate legal safeguards governing the use of firearms and force, the scope for searches and arrests without warrants based on suspicion, an internal complaints resolution mechanism involving a clear conflict of interest, the risk of transferring RAB personnel to the new force without proper vetting, and the provision to include members of the armed forces on deputation, the anti-graft watchdog said in a statement today, Sunday.

In the statement issued to the media, TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman said, “The policy decision to abolish RAB is undoubtedly long overdue, and we wanted to see it as a positive step. But changing the name of a force does not, by itself, constitute institutional reform.”

“Fundamental changes must be made to the structure, personnel, powers, use-of-force provisions and accountability mechanisms of the new force to prevent the recurrence of the serious allegations and evidence of extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and torture associated with RAB,” he stated.

“Otherwise, if a force with the same kind of powers and institutional culture is created under the name of SRB simply by changing RAB’s outer shell, it would amount to little more than repackaging the old institution. The citizens of Bangladesh and the international community cannot be misled by a mere ‘cosmetic makeover’,” he observed.

Referring to the need to amend several provisions of the bill, TIB executive director said, “The bill must permanently close the avenue for members of the armed or defence forces outside the police to be included in the SRB on deputation, as this provision would perpetuate the risk of employing military tactics in internal policing and of training personnel to eliminate opponents, including through killing. At the same time, the draft provides for the wholesale transfer of RAB personnel to the SRB without any form of vetting. In accordance with the United Nations Security Sector Reform (SSR) and Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) standards, a transparent and impartial vetting process must be made mandatory to ensure that no member who was accused of or involved in crimes such as extrajudicial killings, torture or enforced disappearance while serving in RAB can be included in the new force.”

Expressing concern over the conferment of sweeping powers on the force and the absence of judicial safeguards in the draft, Iftekharuzzaman further said, “The draft law grants this specialised unit a wide range of powers, from intelligence surveillance to operations, searches and general investigations. Moreover, the inclusion of vague phrases such as ‘maintaining internal security’ and ‘other duties as directed by the government’ creates scope for suppressing dissent and using force for political purposes, as well as the risk of providing legal cover for extrajudicial killings of the kind seen in the past. Similarly, the draft provides scope for searches and arrests without warrants merely on the basis of suspicion, as well as for maintaining the force’s own detention facilities and interrogation rooms. This constitutes a clear violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution.”

Criticising the complaints resolution mechanism proposed under Section 22 of the draft law or bill, TIB executive director said, “The proposed ‘Complaints Redress Committee’, comprising the Additional Director General and other police officials of the proposed force, is clearly affected by a conflict of interest. A mechanism whereby allegations of serious human rights violations against members of a force are investigated by their own colleagues cannot, in any way, be considered impartial. Instead of this internal mechanism, a completely independent, impartial and conflict-free civilian oversight authority, free from the influence of the police, the executive branch and the force concerned, and comprising human rights and legal experts, must be established to investigate complaints against the force. At the same time, we call for the committee’s investigation report to be made public and for legal safeguards to be incorporated to ensure the rights of affected individuals to compensation and rehabilitation.”

TIB believes that the proposed abolition of RAB presents an important opportunity for the government to establish a genuinely reformed law-enforcement institution.

Unless clear limits are placed on the powers of the new force and independent and impartial oversight, a transparent personnel vetting process, judicial safeguards and effective remedies are ensured, the fundamental objective of abolishing RAB will remain unfulfilled, it said in the statement.

The abolition of RAB must not be limited to changing the name and outer structure of a force; rather, it should mark the beginning of a new law-enforcement system founded on the rule of law, respect for citizens’ rights, effective accountability, and an end to the culture of human rights violations and impunity. This is TIB’s expectation.

TIB has already sent a detailed policy brief, including a section-by-section analysis of the bill and its recommendations, to the relevant minister and the parliamentary committee.

TIB urges that the law be finalised only after giving due consideration to these recommendations and ensuring the meaningful engagement of relevant experts and stakeholders.

item.title: I never considered Salman as anything other than a brother: Shabnur
item.description:
Salman Shah is one of the most iconic heroes in Dhaka’s film industry. Through his acting, style and screen presence, he won people’s hearts in a film career spanning just four years.

After making his film debut with ‘Keyamat Theke Keyamat’ in 1993, he went on to star in 27 films. Even three decades after his death, his popularity has not diminished in the slightest. Instead, Salman Shah seems to have become an even greater subject of discussion over time.

The actor died on 6 September 1996. Thirty years have passed in the blink of an eye. Yet his adored co-star and popular on-screen partner Shabnur still finds it hard to believe that Salman is no longer alive.

She expressed these feelings in a social media post marking the 30th anniversary of Salman Shah’s death.

Salman Shah: What happened in that Eskaton Road flat on Friday

Shabnur wrote, “Even today, I cannot believe that you are no longer here, Salman…” Remembering Salman, she further wrote, “Even after all these years, your memory remains etched in my heart. You were the beloved prince of the screen, the dream hero loved by people. You still live on in our memories and in our love. The immense void your untimely death created in our film industry has still not been filled.”

According to Shabnur, time has passed and generations have changed, but Salman Shah’s popularity and the magic of his acting remain just as alive in people’s hearts. Her final words to her beloved co-star are, “Wherever you are, stay well, dear Salman Shah.”

The Salman-Shabnur pairing was one of the most popular on-screen duos in Dhaka’s film industry. They became so popular with audiences that at one point rumours spread that they were romantically involved. Shabnur, however, has always denied the rumours.

She has said that she always regarded Salman as a brother. Recently, Salman’s mother, Neela Chowdhury, also said that Salman Shah regarded Shabnur as a younger sister.

Shabnur still remembers her first meeting with Salman. She also recalled the memory in an interview with Prothom Alo.

According to Shabnur, “The first time I saw Salman, he was shooting with Moushumi Apu. I would see him while coming and going, but we did not talk much. At the time, I heard that a new hero named Salman Shah had entered the film industry. We were formally introduced while working on the film ‘Tumi Amar’. We became friends through our work. After our first film, ‘Tumi Amar’, was released, it became a superhit.”

Even after Salman’s death, various stories continued to circulate about his relationship with Shabnur. Shabnur is also angry about this.

Salman Shah and Shabnur in love? What Salman’s mother says after 30 years

She said, “It is absolutely true that I never saw Salman in any way other than as a brother. After Salman’s death, some people tried to make a business out of it by involving me in this matter. Some journalists also published various sensational stories about our relationship. I do not know what they gained by doing that. I built my career with a great deal of hard work. I built it bit by bit. Some people tried to enjoy themselves by spreading rumours.”

Shabnur still cannot forget the moment she received the news of Salman’s death. She was at home that day. Suddenly, someone called to tell her that Salman Shah had died. At first, she could not believe it.

“Suddenly, someone called and told me that Salman Shah had died. I scolded them and said, ‘What are you talking about?’ My younger sister went outside and returned after confirming the news of Salman’s death. I was completely stunned. I then went to the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation (BFDC) to see Salman,” Shabnur writes.

item.title: Post-surgery tuberculosis in Pabna: IEDCR begins investigation into cause
item.description:
A team from the government’s Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) has begun investigating the cause of tuberculosis infections found in the surgical wounds of 12 patients following operations at a private hospital in Faridpur, Pabna.

The seven-member team began its work on Sunday morning. The team is led by Md Shahriar Sazzad, director of the National Tuberculosis Control Programme.

On the first day, the team met the 12 patients diagnosed with tuberculosis in their surgical wounds, assessed their physical condition and collected the necessary samples.

Md Shahriar Sazzad, head of the team, said they collected samples from the surgical wounds of all 12 patients on the first day and sent them to Dhaka for testing. They will also gather information about other patients who underwent surgery at the hospital.

He further said while laboratory tests are being conducted, the team will continue its field-level monitoring. On the second day of the investigation, Monday, they will examine the surgical instruments used at the hospital.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Shahriar Sazzad said the investigation was being conducted to determine the cause and severity of the sudden spread of tuberculosis.

“We are examining every aspect and trying to identify the primary source of the infections,” he said. A comprehensive report will be prepared once all laboratory tests have been completed.

According to the report, 12 patients were diagnosed with tuberculosis in their surgical wounds last August after undergoing operations at Al-Madina Lab and Hospital in Faridpur upazila, Pabna. Eleven of them were maternity patients.

Tuberculosis spreading through surgical procedures

After the matter came to light, the upazila health department temporarily closed the hospital’s operation theatre (OT) on 24 August and formed an investigation committee. The matter was also brought to the attention of the IEDCR.

Faridpur Upazila Health and Family Planning Officer Md Rashedul Hasan said the 12 patients infected with tuberculosis are currently receiving treatment under the supervision of Faridpur Upazila Health Complex.

They are being kept under constant observation, and their physical condition is improving with treatment, he added.

Rashedul Hasan further said the health department is also gathering information about other patients who underwent surgery at the hospital in recent months.

item.title: Opposition walks out over ‘weakened’ rights, disappearance bills
item.description:
The opposition walked out of the National Parliament on Sunday in protest against two key human rights bills, accusing the government of backtracking on its promise to introduce stronger safeguards against rights violations and enforced disappearances.
Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman announced the walkout immediately before Parliament began the process of passing the National Human Rights Commission Bill and the Prevention and Redress of Disappearances Bill.
He said the opposition would not participate in passing legislation it considered weaker and more restrictive than the ordinances introduced by the previous interim government.
The confrontation marked the latest escalation of a dispute over the two laws.
When the bills were introduced on August 27, opposition MPs also walked out, arguing that they would not be part of a process that failed to address their core demands for reform.
The opposition subsequently boycotted parliamentary committee discussions on the bills.
It has accused the government of unilaterally repealing the interim government’s ordinances despite concerns raised by victims, stakeholders and domestic and international human rights organizations.
According to the opposition, the government had promised that stronger and more effective legislation would replace the ordinances but ultimately brought bills that weakened their provisions.
Taking the floor on Sunday before the bills were considered, Shafiqur reiterated that position.
“When the bills were lapsed by the Treasury Bench, it was said that they would bring them in a very strong and better form,” he said.
The opposition leader particularly objected to provisions in the proposed National Human Rights Commission law, arguing that they would create different standards for investigating ordinary citizens and members of law enforcement agencies.
“There cannot be a dual application of the law,” he said.
“State forces are employees of the state, but they are citizens of this country. It cannot be that one person can be directly investigated for the same crime, and another person will be stuck in another place.”
Shafiqur said the opposition had therefore decided not to lend legitimacy to the passage of the legislation.
“Since we have already decided that all these laws are being brought in a weak form by lapse, we will not be a partner in passing this law,” he said.
“We are not participating in the discussion of this law and we are now walking out.”
Opposition MPs then left the chamber.

item.title: Dhaka, Delhi eye strengthening cultural engagement
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Sunday met Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury and both sides highlighted the importance of strengthening cultural engagement between the two countries.
The discussion highlighted the deep-rooted cultural connections between the peoples of the two countries.
They discussed potential cooperation and exchanges in the fields of classical music, folk art, heritage conservation, institutional linkages, and joint cultural programmes and conferences, especially as part of Nazrul Borsho celebrations, all aimed at promoting people-to-people ties.
State Minister for Cultural Affairs Ali Nawaz Mahmud Khayyam was also present.

item.title: Woman shot at home: Husband, two others arrested
item.description:
A woman was shot allegedly by her husband at their home in the capital’s Darussalam area on Saturday evening, following an argument, with Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) later arresting three people in connection with the incident.
The arrested are Md Abdul Mannan alias Abdul Hannan, 45, the woman’s husband, Md Rakib, 25, and Md Hatem Mia, 21.
The woman was shot at their home in the Matborbari Mosque Lane area under Darussalam police station, according to RAB. She was initially taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and later shifted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for better treatment. She is currently undergoing treatment there.
RAB-4 said its team visited the scene after the shooting and began an investigation. The three suspects were arrested during a raid in the Darussalam area early Sunday.
RAB said it recovered a foreign-made firearm, a magazine, two rounds of live ammunition and 215 yaba pills from their possession.
According to RAB, Mannan returned home under the influence of drugs on Saturday evening and got into an argument with his wife. At one point, he allegedly shot her with a pistol, seriously injuring her.
After the incident, Mannan allegedly had the firearm taken to the home of his friend Hatem Mia through his son Rakib, RAB said.
The suspects’ locations were later identified using information technology, following which RAB conducted an operation with assistance from Darussalam police, the elite force said.
RAB said Mannan is a listed drug trader and armed criminal who lived with his family as a tenant in a tin-shed house owned by a doctor named Aminul.
The elite force alleged that Mannan used the recovered firearm for drug trading, extortion, intimidation and other criminal activities in Darussalam and surrounding areas.
RAB also claimed that the three arrested suspects face multiple cases at different police stations in the capital, including cases involving drugs, snatching and extortion.
The suspects were handed over to Darussalam police station for legal action.

item.title: Study: What children watch matters more than screen time
item.description:
What children do on screens, and whether parents engage with them, may matter more for language development than simply how many hours they spend on digital devices, according to a study that also reveals widespread passive screen use and limited parental involvement among young children.
Titled “Effect of using screen time in developing children’s speech and language: Bangladesh context,” the MPhil study was conducted by Md Zahid Hossain Khan of Dhaka University’s Department of Communication Disorders under the supervision of Professor Dr Hakim Arif.
The study found that 60% of children surveyed spent at least three hours a day on screens, while 80% primarily watched cartoons and other entertainment content.
Yet only 20% of parents consistently stayed with their children during screen use, highlighting a major gap in how digital devices are being incorporated into children’s daily lives.
Researchers found a striking contrast between un-interative viewing and interactive screen use.
Children aged three to five who used educational and interactive apps repeated new words, asked questions and demonstrated improvements in sentence formation.
Those who mainly watched cartoons or YouTube videos, however, showed less inclination to communicate, with some crying or becoming stubborn when the screen was taken away.
The findings challenge the tendency to judge children’s digital exposure solely by the number of hours spent in front of screens, suggesting that the quality of content, active participation and parental interaction can be critical factors.
The research covered 50 children aged three to eight and an equal number of parents and caregivers in Dhaka, Chittagong and Tangail.
In addition to a survey, researchers directly observed each child for 30 minutes while they used a screen.
The findings show that 40% of the children spent three to four hours a day on screens, while another 20% spent more than four hours.
Mobile phones dominated their digital exposure, used by 90% of the children.
Television was used by 70% and tablets by 50%.
Around 80% primarily watched cartoons and entertainment programs, while 60% of children spend time sitting inactive in front of screens rather than actively interacting with the content.
Among children aged six to eight, researchers observed greater discussion about what they watched, although their sentence structures were comparatively weak.
The study also identified parental involvement as a key concern.
Only one in five parents always accompanied their children during screen use, while just 30% actively regulated screen time.
Half of the parents surveyed believed excessive screen use negatively affected language development, while 60% reported a decline in their children’s vocabulary.
At the same time, 60% believed screens could help children learn language when used appropriately.
“Two-way conversation is a key condition for language learning, while screens can turn communication into a one-way process,” Zahid said.
“If parents sit beside their children and talk about the content, screen time is no longer merely screen time; it becomes part of the learning process.”
The findings therefore suggest that parental engagement can change the nature of screen exposure: rather than children simply consuming content, conversation, questions and responses can turn it into an interactive learning experience.
Professor Saiful Alam Chowdhury of the University of Chittagong said the study recommended age-appropriate limits on screen use, development and promotion of quality educational content in Bangla, training for parents and teachers, and government-led awareness programs.
Professor Dr Hakim Arif said children’s growing exposure to screens had emerged as a major challenge to healthy development.
“There has been little long-term scientific research on the issue in our society. I believe this research will play an important role in addressing that gap,” he said.
The findings point to a broader challenge for parents as digital devices become increasingly embedded in childhood: managing screen use may no longer be simply about limiting hours, but also about determining what children watch, how they interact with it and whether adults remain engaged in the process.

item.title: Death of SB SI in Savar: One arrested
item.description:
Police have arrested a man over the death of a Special Branch (SB) sub-inspector who was allegedly beaten to death during a dispute over parking a private car in Savar’s Aminbazar on Saturday night.
The arrestee suspect has been identified as Zahirul, whom police described as the main accused in the case. Other suspects have also been identified and efforts are underway to arrest them. Savar Model police station Officer-in-Charge Md Saiful Alam confirmed the arrest and the filing of a case on Sunday afternoon.
The victim, Altab Hossain, 58, was working as an SB sub-inspector in Dhaka’s Malibagh zone.
“Zahirul, the main accused who allegedly beat him and was involved in the dispute over the car, has been arrested. The victim’s wife filed the case,” he said.
The OC said police identified the other suspects through the arrested man’s confession, CCTV footage and further investigation.
“Operations are underway to arrest the others,” he added.
The incident took place around 8pm Saturday in the Bardeshi area of Aminbazar.
According to police, an altercation broke out between Altab, his younger son Ariful Islam, 26, and a group of 10–15 people outside a vest factory in the Bardeshi Madina Housing area over the parking of a private car.
At one stage, the group attacked Altab and Ariful, leaving both seriously injured.
Around 9:30pm, they were taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka, where doctors declared Altab dead.
Dhaka District Police Superintendent Shamima Pervin said Altab and his son were attacked while trying to settle a dispute between two sides over parking a private car.
“The sub-inspector and his son were attacked while trying to settle a dispute between two sides over parking a private car. Efforts are underway to arrest those involved,” she said.
Altab was the son of late Jurain Ali Sheikh of Sadhup Para village under Enayetpur police station in Sirajganj. He lived with his family in the Bardeshi Madina City area of Aminbazar.
SB Assistant Sub-Inspector Masud Rana of the Savar zone said Altab was an SB sub-inspector but was not posted in the Savar zone. He said Altab worked in an unspecified SB zone in Dhaka and owned property in Aminbazar.
Police said they launched an operation after receiving information about the attack and arrested Zahirul.
The OC said further details about the case would be disclosed later.

item.title: Body of Bangladeshi killed in Israeli drone strike in Lebanon reaches Satkhira
item.description:
The body of a Bangladeshi worker from Kalaroa upazila of Satkhira, who was killed in a reported Israeli drone strike in Lebanon, reached his village home yesterday morning, plunging his family and neighbours into grief.
The deceased was identified as Shuvo Das of Shripatipur village in the upazila.
His body reached home around 10am, about three months and 25 days after his death in a drone strike in a conflict zone in southern Lebanon on May 11.
Shuvo was the second of four siblings, including three brothers and a sister.
His family said he went to Lebanon about two and a half years ago after selling two decimals of their homestead land to meet the cost of migration. He has now returned home in a coffin, leaving his family devastated.
He was cremated at a local cremation ground after noon.
Shafiqul Islam, of Purbapara village in Sadar upazila, and Nahidul Islam, of Kadakathi village in Ashashuni upazila, of Satkhira were also killed in the Israeli drone strike.
Their bodies reached their respective villages on June 7.
Moin Uddin, a counsellor at the Khulna divisional office of the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, said the government provided the family with a cheque for Tk 85,000 on Saturday night.
He said the family will receive another Tk 3 lakh this month and additional Tk 10 lakh from life insurance after a few months.

item.title: Two-month-old girl dies after alleged beating by father
item.description:
A two-month-old girl allegedly died after being beaten by her father following a marital dispute in the capital’s Darus Salam area.
The baby, Sabiha, died while undergoing treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) around noon on Sunday.
She was allegedly beaten at a rented house in Goiddertek, Darus Salam, around 7:00am on August 22 and admitted to DMCH the same day.
Mohammad Habibur Rahman, inspector-in-charge of the DMCH police outpost, confirmed her death.
Sabia was the daughter of Hridoy Khan of Boheratala village in Shibchar upazila of Madaripur. The family had been living in a rented house in Goiddertek on Mazar Road in Mirpur.
Her mother, Laboni Akter Jannati, said she married Hridoy about one and a half years ago after he divorced his first wife. Hridoy worked at a biryani restaurant.
According to Laboni, they were sleeping together on the day of the incident when Hridoy suddenly began beating the baby. She said he had previously threatened to kill the child and sometimes behaved abnormally. Laboni alleged that Hridoy also pressed the baby’s neck during the assault before fleeing with Tk500 from the house.
She said the baby had injuries on her neck and cheeks. She was rescued and rushed to DMCH, where she died while undergoing treatment on Sunday.
Hridoy has remained missing since the incident, she said.
The body has been kept at the DMCH morgue for autopsy.

item.title: Counterfeit ‘Noorjahan’ products flood Moulvibazar markets
item.description:
Counterfeit versions of "Noorjahan", a popular food brand owned by Ferdous & Sons Corporation, are allegedly flooding markets across Moulvibazar, causing financial losses to the legitimate business owner.
Md Ferdous Bhuiyan Raton, proprietor of the company, alleged that an organized group has been copying the brand name and packaging and selling fake products for nearly 18 months.
He said his company obtained formal approval from the Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution (BSTI) on December 15, 2024, and has been marketing products including Noorjahan Ghee, Butter Oil, Curry Powder and Sauce after complying with government regulations and paying applicable VAT and taxes.
Raton alleged that Iqra Enterprise in Kulaura and Shaha International in Tongi were involved in producing and distributing counterfeit Noorjahan products. He said he lodged a complaint with the Moulvibazar district office of the Directorate of National Consumers’ Right Protection on May 17, 2025, but received no effective remedy.
He later approached the Sylhet regional office of BSTI. Following his complaint, BSTI conducted raids in Kulaura and Barlekha, where the allegations were reportedly substantiated. Iqra Enterprise was fined and instructed to withdraw the counterfeit products from the market.
Raton, however, alleged that the counterfeit products continued to circulate despite the order.
At the same time, several retailers selling genuine Noorjahan products have claimed that they were fined during consumer rights inspections.
Saidur Rahman Chhayad, proprietor of Chhayad Store in Barlekha, said he was fined Tk3,000 on August 24 for selling Noorjahan Ghee. He claimed that although he produced purchase documents, officials told him that the product could not be sold because it was allegedly prohibited.
Atar Ali of Sumiya Store in Kulaura was reportedly fined Tk15,000, while Suman Kapali of Janani Variety Store in Barlekha was fined Tk20,000 after being summoned to the district consumer rights office.
Joni Mia, proprietor of Jannat Store in Juri, also claimed that he was fined Tk15,000 for selling Noorjahan Ghee despite showing documents proving the product's legitimacy.
Tinku Deb of Messrs Joyjit Enterprise in Juri alleged that he was fined Tk15,000 over Noorjahan Butter Oil, although the written fine reportedly mentioned Noorjahan Ghee. He further alleged that he was later asked to pay Tk3,000 as “office expenses”.
Raton claimed that instead of targeting counterfeiters, authorities were harassing legitimate retailers and damaging his business.
“The counterfeit Noorjahan products have flooded the market, yet instead of taking action against counterfeiters, innocent traders selling our genuine products are being harassed and fined,” he said.
A recent visit to markets in Moulvibazar Sadar, Juri, Barlekha, Kulaura and Sreemangal also found various food products allegedly lacking adequate manufacturer and standards information. Among them were several brands of ghee, spices, sauces and butter oil.
Local traders said some suppliers distribute such products to shops on credit and collect payment after they are sold, making it difficult for small retailers to verify the products' legitimacy.
Local SME entrepreneurs have called for transparent and coordinated inspections, arguing that repeated raids and heavy fines could discourage legitimate businesses.
Nurul Islam Kamran, convener of the Moulvibazar Business Forum and former director of the Chamber of Commerce, said traders should follow government regulations but also be given an opportunity to correct minor violations before facing heavy penalties.
“A coordinated inspection system should be introduced instead of separate drives,” he said.
However, Md Al Amin, deputy director of the Moulvibazar district office of the Directorate of National Consumers’ Right Protection, denied allegations of misconduct.
He said fines were imposed after considering the overall circumstances during inspections, rather than solely because a shop was selling a particular product.
Al Amin also denied allegations that officials had instructed traders to stop selling Noorjahan Ghee.
“I did not tell any businessman not to sell Noorjahan Ghee. And it would not be appropriate for me to say that,” he said.
He also rejected allegations that traders were asked to pay money for fake BSTI documents or unofficial expenses.
The proprietor of Iqra Enterprise in Kulaura, Inam Uddin, and the proprietor of Shaha International in Tongi, Mostafizur Rahman Munim, could not be reached by phone when calls were made to them around 5pm on Saturday.
Contact attempts were made to seek their comments on the matter, but neither of them answered the calls.
Moulvibazar Deputy Commissioner Md Touhiduzzaman Pavel said: “I have received a written complaint regarding the matter. The issue will be investigated and necessary action will be taken.”

“We will collect samples of the water and fish through the upazila fisheries officer and conduct tests,” he said.

item.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel conflicts
item.description:
The world’s food system is coming under mounting pressure from climate change, extreme weather, wars and trade disruptions, with new research warning that shifts in agricultural productivity could increase risks of conflict and displacement — particularly in vulnerable regions such as South Asia and the Sahel.
The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI), developed by researchers Laura Mayoral and Hannes Mueller, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity worldwide.
“The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions,” said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and Barcelona School of Economics.
Hundreds of millions of people already live in areas producing less food than 30 years ago. Within 25 years, nearly half the world’s population could live in areas where agricultural productivity has declined.
Droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests, while wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting food, fuel and fertiliser supplies.
The Ukraine war has repeatedly unsettled grain markets, while disruption surrounding the Strait of Hormuz has increased fuel and fertiliser costs.
But researchers found that declining production is not the only potential source of conflict.
Rising agricultural productivity can also create tensions by making previously marginal land more valuable.
“If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today,” Mueller said.
Large agricultural companies are already buying land expected to become more productive in coming decades, potentially driving up prices and displacing local communities.
The research suggests such agricultural shifts are more likely to fuel violence in non-democratic countries, while democratic institutions can provide mechanisms for competing groups to negotiate over changing access to land and resources.
South Asia is particularly vulnerable, according to Abdullah Fahimi of the German Council on Foreign Relations.
“The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel,” he said, citing the combination of climate vulnerability and rapid population growth.
Home to around two billion people, South Asia depends heavily on vulnerable water systems as well as imported food. At the same time, domestic agriculture faces intensifying heatwaves, floods, declining land productivity and saltwater intrusion.
The Himalayas and Hindu Kush, which provide crucial water for agriculture and drinking across the region, are also undergoing rapid changes as glaciers and snow melt.
In the short term, melting could increase water availability. Later this century, however, Fahimi warned of “a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people.”
Food insecurity can also drive migration, undermine confidence in governments and create opportunities for armed groups to recruit people whose livelihoods have collapsed.
Researchers stress that climate change and food shortages do not automatically cause violence. The decisive factor may be whether institutions can manage disputes over increasingly scarce -- or newly valuable -- land, water and livelihoods.
Climate adaptation, they argue, therefore cannot be limited to new crops and technologies.
Where institutions cannot peacefully manage the redistribution of resources and opportunities, pressure on the food system could ultimately become pressure on peace itself.
